Notes: 1 Maccabees 13:43-48 (year 170 SE = 142/1 BCE, 13:41). Simon besieged and took Gazara and expelled its gentile inhabitants. He cleansed the houses of idols and 'settled in it men who observed the law', then fortified it and built himself a house there. This is the founding of the Jewish (Judean) settlement at Hasmonean Gezer. Josephus, Ant. 13.215, also records that Simon 'subdued the city of Gazara'. No numbers given. [Review fix: Year Established -950 basis: c. 950 BCE Gezer became an Israelite royal stronghold under Solomon (1 Kings 9:15-17); Encyclopaedia Judaica adds that its population stayed mostly Canaanite. This note was on a Persian-period jar-handle row deleted in review because jar handles show an administrative tie, not Judean residents]

1 Maccabees 13:53 (171 SE = May 141 BCE). Simon made his son John (Hyrcanus) commander of all the forces, 'and he dwelt in Gazara'. Gezer became the Hasmonean military headquarters, with a Hasmonean leader resident there. No numbers given.

1 Maccabees 14:34, the honorific decree for Simon (172 SE = Sept. 140 BCE). He fortified Joppa and Gazara, 'on the borders of Azotus, where the enemy formerly dwelt'. 'He settled Jews there, and provided in those cities whatever was necessary for their restoration.' This is Jewish settlement by Hasmonean policy. No numbers given.

Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Gezer' (Jewish Virtual Library). Gezer stayed in Greek hands until Simon took it in 142 BCE and expelled the foreigners. He made it the military centre of his state under his son John Hyrcanus, and it was Simon's residence for a time. A Hasmonean palace found there was apparently built by Greek prisoners of war. A curse scratched on one stone reads 'May fire descend from heaven and devour the house of Simeon'. The palace date is approximate (c. 140 BCE, under Simon). No population figure.

Bible History Daily (BAS) on the 13th known Gezer boundary stone, a bilingual stone found in 2012. It is dated to the period of conflict between the Seleucids and the Maccabees, so the year is c. -140 and approximate. The excavators' press release says the stones show the Jewish occupants' concern with 'keeping their fields according to Jewish law'. It points to a Jewish farming community; no numbers given.

1 Maccabees 15:28 and 15:35 (174 SE = 139/8 BCE). Antiochus VII Sidetes demanded that Simon hand back 'Joppa and Gazara and the citadel in Jerusalem'. Simon refused and offered only payment. Gazara was still held by the Jews. No numbers given.

1 Maccabees 16:1, 16:19-21 (177 SE = Jan./Feb. 134 BCE). John 'went up from Gazara' to report to Simon. After Simon was murdered at Dok, Ptolemy son of Abubus 'sent other men to Gazara to do away with John'. Messengers reported the murders to 'John at Gazara'. Gezer was John Hyrcanus's seat. No numbers given.

Josephus, Ant. 13.261, the senatus consultum before the praetor Fannius. Envoys of the Jewish people under the high priest Hyrcanus asked that 'Joppa and its harbours and Gazara and Pegae' be restored to the Jews, because Antiochus (VII) had taken them in war against a Senate decree. Josephus gives no year; the date of the decree is disputed, so c. 130 BCE is approximate. This implies a temporary Seleucid hold on Gazara under Hyrcanus. The source does not say whether the Jewish settlers stayed. No numbers given.

Ronny Reich, 'The Boundary of Gezer: On the Jewish Settlement at Gezer in Hasmonean Times', Eretz-Israel 18 (1985) 167-179 (abstract only). The bilingual boundary inscriptions read Hebrew tḥm gzr ('boundary of Gezer') and Greek Alkiou. Reich dates them most plausibly to the end of the 2nd and beginning of the 1st c. BCE, so -100 is used. He reads the enclosed c. 4 sq km area as the farmland of the new observant Jewish community settled after the Hasmonean conquest, an enclave within gentile-owned land, possibly marked for priestly offerings. Organized Jewish farming community; no population figure.

Archaeology in Israel: Gezer (Jewish Virtual Library). After Simon's conquest the Iron Age fortifications were restored and semicircular towers added. 'Evidence of a Jewish population during this period includes several stepped pools for ritual bathing (mikva'ot).' The year is the Hasmonean-period midpoint (-90) because no closer date is given. Several miqvaot point to a resident Jewish community; no numbers given.

Chabad.org article citing S. Ortiz and S. Wolff, 'Gezer', Encyclopedia of the Bible and Its Reception 10 (2015). The last known occupation of Tel Gezer dates to the Maccabean rulers. The authors report 'evidence of a possible mikveh that was found in a Jewish home from that period'. The year is the Hasmonean-period midpoint (-90), approximate. Domestic Jewish occupation on the tell; no numbers given.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) 'Gezer': 'Under Gabinius, Gazara (Greek, "Gadara") became the chief town of its district', meaning one of the five Jewish synedria set up by Gabinius in 57 BCE (Josephus, Ant. 14.91; War 1.170). Josephus's text reads 'Gadara', and scholars are divided on identifying it with Gazara, so this is uncertain. If correct, Gezer was a Jewish administrative centre. No numbers given.

BibleWalks, citing B.-Z. Rosenfeld (1988). Rosenfeld dates the Gezer boundary markers to the reign of Herod the Great, which differs from the Hasmonean dating; the Herodian-period midpoint -20 is used. The Hebrew 'boundary of Gezer' wording implies Jewish landholders. The page also discusses and rejects the view that they were Sabbath-limit markers. No numbers given.

Archaeology in Israel: Gezer (Jewish Virtual Library). Under Herod, Gezer lost its role as a frontier town, and until 70 CE it was a private estate marked by rock inscriptions reading 'boundary of Gezer'. The year is the Herodian midpoint (-20), approximate. This suggests a reduced, estate-based settlement; the source does not say whether its farmers were Jewish. No numbers given.

World History Encyclopedia 'Gezer'. After the Maccabean period the city 'may have been temporarily deserted'. 'Gezer seems to have been part of the estate of a Greek landowner named Alkios. It was apparently farmed by Jewish settlers who lived on the land.' The inscribed boundary stones 'may belong to the Roman period', and the tell may then have been uninhabited apart from tombs and other structures. The year is the early-Roman midpoint (4), approximate. Small Jewish farming population on the estate; no numbers given.
